Temporal Awareness Is the Missing State Variable for Agents

Why agents don't have agency yet — and why no smarter model will fix it

Working Memory. Script/essay v3. Spine: agency needs a sense of time; agents don't have one; it's architectural, not a model-quality problem; the fix is to make the state transition — not the fact — the unit of memory, and to maintain elapsed time in a runtime layer. Every empirical claim is grounded in a cited paper or an experiment I ran (marked [EXP]). Production cues in [brackets].

0. The reason to care

We keep saying we want agents. Systems that don't just answer, but act — notice something changed, pick up a dropped thread, check back when a fact goes stale, interrupt you when a plan is slipping. Agency.

And after two years of staggering progress, the best proactivity we have is still a cron job. A timer that fires whether or not anything happened. Everything genuinely proactive an "agent" does today is either a human poking it, or a clock someone hard-coded.

The usual explanation is "the models aren't smart enough yet." I think that's wrong, and I want to show you why with experiments you can rerun. The bottleneck isn't intelligence. It's that we've given these systems reasoning, tools, memory, and retrieval — and withheld the one thing agency actually requires: a sense that time is passing. An agent can't decide when to act if it has no internal model of when it is.

This is a missing state variable, not a missing IQ. And once you see it, you see it everywhere.

1. Two words wearing one mask: awareness vs. reasoning

First, a distinction the field keeps blurring, because the whole argument depends on it.

Temporal reasoning is logic about time: ordering events, computing that three days before Friday is Tuesday, inferring which fact came first. It's analysis. And it's improving — you can train it.

Temporal awareness is perception of time: knowing how much has elapsed, sensing that a fact may now be stale, feeling a deadline tighten. It's not deduction; it's a state you're in.

A clean way to hold them apart: reasoning tells you what happened and in what order; awareness tells you where you are in time right now, and what that means for what's still true. You can be a brilliant temporal reasoner and completely time-unaware — like someone who can solve any calendar puzzle but has no idea it's been three hours since lunch.

[SCREEN: the angry vs. vegetarian example — keep it on screen through §2]

Here's the one-sentence version. Tell an assistant "I'm angry" and "I'm vegetarian." In a flat vector store these become the same kind of object: a fact, written once, true forever. But "angry" is true for an hour; "vegetarian" is true for years. The difference between them isn't logical — it's temporal validity, and the store has no axis for it. Reasoning can't recover what the representation threw away.

2. The evidence: three failures, one cause

Let me show you the same failure in three different settings, because once looks like a quirk and three times shows it's structural. For each, the setup matters more than the headline number — so I'll tell you exactly what was tested.

(a) Planning — and this one starts with us. [EXP — I ran this] In 1979, Kahneman and Tversky named the planning fallacy: people systematically underestimate how long their own tasks will take — on average by about 2.5× — even when they've done the same task before. The mechanism is well studied: when we plan, we build a best-case story of the work and silently delete the friction — the bug we'll hit, the meeting that runs long, the dependency that breaks. We plan the idealized path, not the real one.

Now connect that to language models. They're trained on our writing, and our writing is full of optimistic plans — quarterly roadmaps, "Week 1 / Week 2 / Week 3" project schedules. So they don't just inherit the human bias, they inherit its format. I tested this directly: I gave GPT-4o a task an autonomous agent finishes in about ten minutes — "write a script that emails me the weather" — and asked it to plan the work. It returned an eight-day schedule, budgeting a full day for "email the formatted weather data." [SHOW the terminal output] It can do the task in one turn; it just reproduces the shape of a human plan instead of estimating how long the work actually takes, because it has no internal clock telling it "for me, this is ten minutes."

(b) Acting while the world keeps moving — Robotouille (Cornell, arXiv 2502.05227). Robotouille is a kitchen simulator where an agent completes recipes — chop, cook, assemble. It has two modes. In the synchronous mode, every action finishes instantly: you "cook the patty" and it's done before your next decision. In the asynchronous mode, actions take real time — the patty cooks for several steps — so the agent must start other work and return, tracking what's in progress. The second mode is just ordinary life: things happen while you're busy. A standard ReAct agent (the loop where the model thinks → acts → observes → repeats) scores 47% synchronous and 11% asynchronous — same recipes, same model, the only change being that time now passes during the task. It can sequence instant steps; it falls apart the moment it has to hold "the patty has been cooking for three steps" as a live, advancing fact while doing something else.

(c) Behaving under a deadline — Real-Time Deadlines (UPenn, Sehgal et al., arXiv 2601.13206). Two language models negotiate a deal — buyer and seller haggling over price — under a deadline expressed two ways. In the turn-budget condition, the model is told it has a fixed number of messages left: a discrete countdown it can literally read in the conversation. In the wall-clock condition, it's told it has a fixed number of seconds — real time, which elapses whether or not tokens are being generated. The result: under turn budgets the models close deals in time almost perfectly — they can count messages. Under wall-clock deadlines, GPT-5.1-chat-latest closes only 4% of deals; it runs out of time without noticing. Inject the remaining seconds at the top of every turn and closure jumps to 32% (odds of acceptance ×6.4, p<0.001). The authors' diagnosis is exact: the models "respond to urgency cues but cannot generate them internally." [SHOW: highlight this line on the paper] The strategy was never missing. An internal estimate of elapsed real time was.

The common thread. In all three the model has the competence — it can write the script, plan the recipe, run the negotiation. What it lacks is one maintained quantity: how much time has passed, and how much remains. That is a missing state variable — a value a system is supposed to keep current as the world changes — not a gap in reasoning. A perception failure, not a logic failure.

3. Why no smarter model fixes this

It's tempting to assume scale eats this. I don't think it does, and the reason is architectural, not anecdotal.

A transformer processes a sequence of discrete tokens with positional encodings. Position is which token, not what time. There is simply no mechanism in the stack for the proposition "time is passing right now while I sit idle." Between your 9am message and your 5pm message, the model experiences one token of separation — not eight hours. It can read a timestamp string you hand it, but reading "14:00" is not the same as having waited.

This is what the Token-Time Hypothesis names directly: LLMs treat tokens as the unit of time and try to infer wall-clock time from the length and sequence of text. Token-time and wall-clock-time are two different measurement systems, and the model only has the first. [cite: "Can LLMs map token time to continuous wall-clock time?" — verify ID before publishing]

That's why temporal awareness looks orthogonal to reasoning ability. The deadline study makes it concrete: turn-budgets (token-time) → near-perfect; wall-clock deadlines (real time) → collapse. Same model, same strategic competence, one axis it can't perceive. You can scale reasoning forever and never grow a clock, because the clock was never a property of the architecture. The two honest fixes are (i) change the architecture to carry continuous-time state, or (ii) maintain time outside the model and feed it in as a conditioning signal. Most of the field is quietly doing a degenerate version of (ii) — pasting a timestamp in the prompt — and the TicToc result (Univ. of Maryland, arXiv 2510.23853) shows the ceiling on that: even with timestamps, no model exceeds 65% alignment with human timing judgments, then it plateaus. Prompting can't manufacture a sense it doesn't have.

4. The cognitive-science frame (why "store the fact" is the wrong primitive)

Step back to how memory actually works in the one system we know does this well: us.

Endel Tulving (1985) defined episodic memory as the capacity for mental time travel — to re-experience a moment in time. Getting there takes three processes: encoding (turn experience into a representation of a moment), consolidation (store it durably), retrieval (re-enter it later). Every one of those is timestamped by construction. And human memory comes in kinds — procedural, semantic, episodic — across durations — sensory, short-term, long-term. Time is not metadata on human memory; it's the scaffolding.

Now look at what we built instead. We took the richest of these — episodic, temporal, experiential — and flattened it into a vector: a point with no "when," no validity, no successor. Tokens and embeddings are time-blind by default. We didn't model memory; we modeled a filing cabinet.

Here's the idea I actually want to test, and it falls straight out of Tulving:

The unit of memory is not the fact. It is not the chunk. It is the state transition.

A useful memory shouldn't store "user is vegetarian." It should store the transition: was → became, when, how fast, what it implies now. Because the highest-value intelligence isn't the current state — it's the delta. That the user changed from "vegetarian" to "pescatarian" matters more than either snapshot, and current systems destroy it: conflict-resolution that just overwrites the old value with the new one throws away the trajectory. Overwriting Monday's belief with Friday's loses the most valuable thing in the data — that something moved. Memory is not a snapshot. It's a trajectory of transitions, each with a validity window. "I am busy" isn't true forever; it's true for two hours. A system that stores transitions can ask the question a flat store can't: is this still true?

5. The fix — and it's more than injecting a timestamp

[SCREEN: build this up as three layers, bottom = what you can build now]

So what do you actually build? Three layers, increasing depth:

Layer 1 — explicit time injection. Put the clock in the prompt. This is what almost everyone does. It helps a little (4%→32% on the deadline task) and ceilings hard (≤65% on TicToc). Necessary, not sufficient. Don't stop here.

Layer 2 — transition memory (a temporal world model). Make the store itself temporal: every fact carries created_at, valid_until (estimated from its type — moods decay in minutes, diets in years), and a link to what it replaced. Retrieval returns not "user is vegetarian" but "user became pescatarian 3 weeks ago (was vegetarian 2 yrs); diet beliefs update ~yearly, so: current, high-confidence." This is buildable today, and it's the version of memory cog-sci says is right. [GROUND: PIE already stores 6,716 state transitions over your own life — this isn't hypothetical, it's the substrate you have.]

Layer 3 — a Temporal MCP: a runtime control plane. The missing state variable lives outside the model, in a layer that (1) maintains elapsed time as a first-class signal, (2) tracks a current-world-state the model can read and write mid-conversation, and (3) fires proactively — not on a cron, but when the temporal model says a fact expired, a plan slipped, or a thread went quiet too long. This is the thing that turns "answer when asked" into "act when warranted." This is where agency comes from.

[SCREEN: contrast — cron job (fires on a fixed timer, blind) vs. temporal control plane (fires when state changes meaning)]

The architectural fix (continuous-time hidden states, micro-turn models like TML's) is real and coming, but it means training new models. Layers 2 and 3 you can ship on top of the models we already have.

6. What this unlocks

This isn't a niche memory tweak. The missing clock is load-bearing for everything people actually want from agents:

  • Proactivity → agency. An agent can only decide when to interrupt, recheck, or surface something if it maintains time. No temporal state, no real initiative — just cron jobs wearing a trench coat.
  • Multi-agent orchestration. A real orchestrator needs to know what each subagent is doing at each point in time to resolve conflicts and sequence work. Without a temporal store of subagent state, "orchestration" is just fan-out and pray. (This is the same transition-memory primitive, applied to agents instead of facts.)
  • Async planning. Robotouille's 47→11 collapse is exactly this: interleaving real-duration actions. A temporal world model is the missing piece.
  • Continual learning. Pausing to update a belief is trivial if memory is a trajectory of transitions — you append a transition, you don't overwrite. The hard version of "time-aware" Karpathy keeps pointing at (updating across sessions) gets much easier when the substrate is built this way.

Different surfaces, same engine: web agents, an enterprise/org world model, sales motions, a life-sim assistant — each is a stream of unstructured human↔agent conversation that needs to become a temporal world model, not a pile of timeless facts.

7. Close

We've been trying to make agents more agentic by making the model smarter. But agency was never only an intelligence problem. It's a time problem. An agent with no sense of elapsed time can't be proactive, can't orchestrate, can't know when it's wrong — no matter how well it reasons.

The fix isn't a better prompt or a bigger model. It's giving the system the state variable we forgot to include: a real, maintained sense of when. Build memory as a trajectory of transitions, maintain elapsed time in a control plane the model can act on, and "answer when asked" becomes "act when it matters."

The next frontier model card will have a row for time. The next useful agent will have a clock it actually runs on.
